verses.text: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.
If I dole out all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.
Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,
doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;
bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.
For we know in part and we prophesy in part;
but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.
But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.

1.title: Patience, Kindness, and the Architecture of Agape
1.historicalBackground: Though frequently read at weddings, 1 Corinthians 13 was originally written to a fractious urban congregation in Roman Corinth—a bustling port city obsessed with status, rhetorical brilliance, and spiritual prestige.
1.theologicalContext: Every single descriptor of love in verses 4–7 is written in Greek as an active verb rather than an abstract noun: love acts patiently, acts kindly, keeps no ledger of wrongs.
1.practicalApplication: Notice the phrase "takes no account of evil" (verse 5)—an accounting term for keeping a ledger of offenses. Ask yourself today: what grievance am I still tallying that grace invites me to close?
1.reflectionPrayer: God of steadfast love, strip away my pride and impatience. Teach me to keep no ledger of wrongs, to rejoice in truth, and to carry your gentle endurance into every room I enter today. Amen.

3.title: Patience, Kindness, and the Architecture of Agape
3.historicalBackground:
Though frequently read at weddings, 1 Corinthians 13 was originally written to a fractious urban congregation in Roman Corinth—a bustling port city obsessed with status, rhetorical brilliance, and spiritual prestige.

Paul places this lyrical hymn directly between chapters 12 and 14, where members were competing over who possessed the most impressive gifts. Corinth prized polished bronze gongs and theatrical speech; Paul calls loveless eloquence mere noise.
3.theologicalContext:
Every single descriptor of love in verses 4–7 is written in Greek as an active verb rather than an abstract noun: love acts patiently, acts kindly, keeps no ledger of wrongs.

Agape is not a fragile emotion dependent on compatibility; it is the durable posture of God’s own character extending patience toward imperfect people.
3.practicalApplication:
Notice the phrase "takes no account of evil" (verse 5)—an accounting term for keeping a ledger of offenses. Ask yourself today: what grievance am I still tallying that grace invites me to close?

Practice "macrothumia" (long-tempered patience) in one frustrating conversation today: pause before replying, listen without self-defense, and choose kindness over winning an argument.
3.reflectionPrayer: God of steadfast love, strip away my pride and impatience. Teach me to keep no ledger of wrongs, to rejoice in truth, and to carry your gentle endurance into every room I enter today. Amen.

lyrics.title: The Greatest of These
verse1: If I should speak in silver tongues
Without Your love my loudest praise
Is hollow brass and fading gold.
chorus: Love is patient, love is kind,
Keeps no ledger of the wrong;
Through every shadow we see dim,
verse2: It bears the weight, it hopes the best,
It lays its own advantage down,
Rejoicing where the truth takes root
Without a boast or borrowed crown.
bridge: Faith will anchor, hope will rise,
Until we see You face to face;
And greatest still of all that stays
Is love, unending in Your grace.
